Explore lexical composition with CA and MDS

Source: vignettes/lexical-ordination.Rmd
lexical-ordination.Rmd

Which documents use similar vocabulary, and which words help explain their differences? Correspondence analysis (CA) describes a document-by-term count table. Classical multidimensional scaling (MDS, also called principal coordinates analysis or PCoA) represents a chosen set of document dissimilarities. The choice of dissimilarity defines what “similar” means; a map does not establish semantic similarity, proficiency, a causal effect, or a statistically significant group.

This guide uses ldfreq 0.3.0.9018 or later. Its helpers are explicitly sourced installed examples, not exported functions. MDS uses R’s stats::cmdscale(); CA requires the optional ca package (install.packages("ca")). No new tokenizer or model is needed. The example uses authored counts to make the calculations checkable, not empirical learner differences.

Begin with the counted documents 

library(ldfreq)
demo <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "lexical-ordination-demo.R",
  package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), demo)
helper <- demo$helper
tab <- demo$tab
print(tab$documents, row.names = FALSE)
#>  document_id requested source_tokens kept_tokens missing_terms counted_tokens
#>           d1      TRUE             8           7             0              7
#>           d2      TRUE             6           6             0              6
#>           d3      TRUE             7           7             0              7
#>           d4      TRUE             6           6             0              6
#>           d5      TRUE             6           6             0              6
#>           d6      TRUE             6           6             0              6
#>           d7      TRUE             7           7             0              7
#>      partial      TRUE             2           2             1              1
#>        empty      TRUE             0           0             0              0
#>      removed      TRUE             1           0             0              0
#>      outside     FALSE             1           1             0              0
#>              status active_tokens
#>              active             7
#>              active             6
#>              active             7
#>              active             6
#>              active             6
#>              active             6
#>              active             7
#>    incomplete_terms             0
#>        empty_source             0
#>  no_selected_tokens             0
#>       not_requested             0
tab$active_counts
#>    learn read write speak tree river rain wind
#> d1     4    2     1     0    0     0    0    0
#> d2     3    1     0     2    0     0    0    0
#> d3     0    0     0     0    4     2    1    0
#> d4     0    0     0     0    2     0    3    1
#> d5     2    0     2     0    0     2    0    0
#> d6     0    3     0     2    1     0    0    0
#> d7     1    4     2     0    0     0    0    0

Seven documents contribute 45 tokens. partial has an unavailable selected lemma, so its entire profile is excluded. empty has no source tokens, removed has no selected tokens, and outside was not requested. These states remain separate. counts retains available counts for all requested documents; active_counts contains exactly the complete, nonempty profiles fitted below. The former must not be silently substituted for the latter.

The source, original token rows and selection mask are retained. The recipe does not normalize case or Unicode, infer lemmas, combine documents, or treat missing labels as absence. Word identity is the exact selected string.

For your own unchanged lexdiv_import_annotations() result, load the helpers explicitly and supply IDs and a selection rule. The annotation guide describes source-aligned inputs.

helper <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
for (file in c("concordance.R", "lexical-ordination.R"))
  sys.source(system.file("examples", file, package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), helper)
tab <- helper$ordination_table(
  annotations, document_ids = study_document_ids,
  preprocessing_id = "lemma-exclude-punctuation-v1",
  term_col = "lemma", keep = keep,
  min_count = 1L, min_documents = 1L
)

keep has one nonmissing logical value per original token. The preprocessing label describes a policy; it does not prove that different annotation pipelines are equivalent. The minimum count and document-frequency thresholds use the requested documents with complete selected terms and are applied once, before fitting. features retains counts and selection decisions. A document with no retained features remains in the audit as no_selected_features.

Thresholds change the analyzed vocabulary and hence the geometry. Choose them for the research question and report them; do not tune them to make groups separate. The default retains every term in the complete selected profiles. The example bounds dense document-term and document-distance matrices using max_cells = 1e6; it is intended for a bounded research collection.

CA: inspect the words that define the configuration 

has_ca <- requireNamespace("ca", quietly = TRUE)
if (has_ca) {
  ca_result <- helper$ordination_ca(tab, k = 2)
  print(ca_result$axes)
  print(ca_result$diagnostics)
  first_axis <- subset(ca_result$columns, axis == 1)
  print(first_axis[order(first_axis$contribution, decreasing = TRUE), ], row.names = FALSE)
}
#>   axis   eigenvalue inertia_fraction

#>

#> [1] 2
#>

#> [1] 8.410747e-11
#> 
#>     id axis coordinate       mass contribution       cos2
#>   rain    1 -1.6959986 0.08888889   0.30399319 0.79447114
#>   tree    1 -1.1870903 0.15555556   0.26062645 0.75582475
#>  learn    1  0.6909648 0.22222222   0.12614347 0.44709388
#>   read    1  0.6583431 0.22222222   0.11451372 0.41847030

#>  river    1 -0.4622453 0.08888889   0.02258177 0.08608317

CA compares row profiles using column marginal frequencies and weights documents by their token totals. Longer documents therefore have greater mass; it does not make all documents equally influential. The rows and columns tables report principal coordinates, mass, contribution (a proportion, not a percentage) and cos². Contribution describes a point’s role in an axis. Cos² describes how well that axis represents the point; it is NA for points with numerically zero distance to the centroid. A distant rare word need not contribute much.

if (has_ca) helper$ordination_plot(ca_result)

if (has_ca) helper$ordination_plot(ca_result, which = "terms", monochrome = TRUE)

Document and term maps are separate principal-coordinate maps. Do not compare their plotted row-to-column distances as if they measured association. In these authored documents, the school-related and nature-related words help explain the dominant contrast; this is a vocabulary-composition description, not a validated topic or ability scale. Read the contributions and cos² before naming an axis. CA has at most min(documents - 1, terms - 1) nontrivial dimensions; rank-one inputs receive a one-dimensional display. Identical profiles have no nonzero CA inertia and are reported as not analyzable.

MDS: choose the meaning of dissimilarity

Jaccard dissimilarity is 1 - shared types / union types. Hellinger distance here is the Euclidean distance between square-root relative-frequency profiles, without the optional 1/sqrt(2) scaling. Jaccard ignores repetition. Hellinger retains differences in allocation among words. Neither removes the sampling uncertainty of short documents; Jaccard also depends on the observed type sets.

jaccard <- helper$ordination_mds(tab, distance = "jaccard", k = 2)
hellinger <- helper$ordination_mds(tab, distance = "hellinger", k = 2)
as.matrix(jaccard$distance)["d1", "d7"]
#> [1] 0
as.matrix(hellinger$distance)["d1", "d7"]
#> [1] 0.4651756

d1 and d7 use exactly the same types, so their Jaccard distance is zero. Their allocation of tokens differs, so their Hellinger distance is positive. These results answer different questions; they do not show that one distance is universally better. The original distance object retains document labels. Directional coverage is not a symmetric distance and is not accepted here.

helper$ordination_plot(hellinger)

MDS axes are coordinates, not automatically interpretable lexical traits. Their sign or orientation can change while all interpoint distances remain identical. The plotting helper uses equal axis units and returns the plotted data invisibly. Use monochrome = TRUE for black and white. Group labels, if added, must be matched by document ID and do not test a group effect. Repeated observations retain their writer/task/occasion information separately; MDS does not model their dependence. Independently fitted maps cannot be compared by raw coordinates.

head(hellinger$pairs)
#>   document_a document_b original_distance fitted_distance
#> 1         d1         d2         0.7032206       0.4171164
#> 2         d1         d3         1.4142136       1.3287895
#> 3         d1         d4         1.4142136       1.3740066
#> 4         d1         d5         0.8310792       0.6533169
#> 5         d1         d6         1.1153793       0.9877046
#> 6         d1         d7         0.4651756       0.1626916

distance_rmse is the root mean squared difference between the original and plotted distances. relative_distance_error divides their sum of squared errors by the sum of squared original distances before taking the square root; it is not NMDS stress. The example’s Jaccard matrix has a negative eigenvalue. Its negative magnitude relative to total absolute eigenvalue magnitude is retained, with a relative eigenvalue tolerance of 1e-10. No additive correction or silent distance transformation is applied. Non-Euclidean geometry and omission of positive dimensions can both prevent distance reconstruction. There is no automatic acceptability threshold for the resulting map.

with(hellinger$pairs, {
  plot(original_distance, fitted_distance, asp = 1, pch = 16, col = "#0072B2",
    xlab = "Original Hellinger distance", ylab = "Distance in two-dimensional map")
  abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
})

This plot overlays the identity line on the original and reproduced distances. Inspect pairs far from that line before interpreting local neighborhoods. All-zero distances have no nontrivial configuration. Zero distances between some nonempty documents are retained, not replaced by arbitrary small positive values. The recipe exposes the requested and effective dimension counts and any recorded rank warning from cmdscale().

Return to the evidence and save the complete analysis 

helper$ordination_occurrences(tab, "learn")
#>    document_id segment_id token_index start end token_row  term
#> 1           d1         s1           1     1   5         1 learn
#> 2           d1         s1           2     7  11         2 learn
#> 3           d1         s1           3    13  17         3 learn
#> 4           d1         s1           4    19  23         4 learn
#> 8           d2         s1           1     1   5         9 learn
#> 9           d2         s1           2     7  11        10 learn
#> 10          d2         s1           3    13  17        11 learn
#> 27          d5         s1           1     1   5        28 learn
#> 28          d5         s1           2     7  11        29 learn
#> 39          d7         s1           1     1   5        40 learn
#>                                         text surface
#> 1  learn learn learn learn read read write .   learn
#> 2  learn learn learn learn read read write .   learn
#> 3  learn learn learn learn read read write .   learn
#> 4  learn learn learn learn read read write .   learn
#> 8         learn learn learn read speak speak   learn
#> 9         learn learn learn read speak speak   learn
#> 10        learn learn learn read speak speak   learn
#> 27       learn learn river river write write   learn
#> 28       learn learn river river write write   learn
#> 39     learn read read read read write write   learn
pair <- lexdiv_term_overlap(
  colnames(tab$active_counts)[tab$active_counts["d1", ] > 0],
  colnames(tab$active_counts)[tab$active_counts["d3", ] > 0],
  document_ids = c("d1", "d3"), measures = "jaccard_types", details = "terms"
)
pair$shared_terms
#> [1] term          token_count_a token_count_b
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
pair$unique_to_a
#>    term token_count_a
#> 1 learn             1
#> 2  read             1
#> 3 write             1
pair$unique_to_b
#>    term token_count_b
#> 1  rain             1
#> 2 river             1
#> 3  tree             1

Occurrence rows retain document, segment, token and character offsets plus the original text. Optional context searches can use the existing concordance workflow, with the saved active token mask. The pair comparison above verifies the type-based interpretation; it does not reproduce Hellinger distance because that distance uses frequencies.

record <- list(table = tab, ca = if (has_ca) ca_result else NULL,
  jaccard = jaccard, hellinger = hellinger, session = sessionInfo())
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds") # Choose a persistent private path for your study.
saveRDS(record, path, version = 2)
reopened <- readRDS(path)
helper$ordination_validate(reopened$table)
helper$ordination_validate(reopened$jaccard)
stopifnot(identical(reopened, record))

In another R session, load the package and the two helper files as shown above, read the saved RDS, validate its records and call helper$ordination_occurrences(reopened$table, "learn") or helper$ordination_plot(reopened$hellinger). The saved table contains source texts; keep it under the same access restrictions as those texts. A CSV of coordinates is useful for display but does not replace this record.

A report should state the observational unit and included IDs, token/lemma and selection policy, excluded-document counts and reasons, feature thresholds, distance or CA weighting, dimensions, diagnostics and software versions. For example: “We retained seven complete nonempty profiles (45 tokens), excluding one document with a missing selected lemma, one empty source and one document without selected tokens. We described lexical composition by CA and examined type sharing and frequency composition with separately defined MDS distances.” Add the actual inertia and distance-reconstruction diagnostics from the saved results and describe their implications. Do not turn this authored example into an empirical claim about learner development.

MCA, nonmetric MDS, automatic feature/distance selection and inferential tests are outside this recipe. CA and weighted PCoA with chi-square distances can describe the same geometry; agreement between such maps is not independent validation.

References

  • Nenadic, O., & Greenacre, M. (2007). Correspondence analysis in R, with two- and three-dimensional graphics: The ca package. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(3), 1–13.
  • R Core Team. Classical multidimensional scaling: cmdscale.
  • Legendre, P., & Gallagher, E. D. (2001). Ecologically meaningful transformations for ordination of species data. Oecologia, 129, 271–280. Transformation definitions.
